items.title: HFIR rotates ARKK put profits into Dec $60 BNO calls: 'Q4 oversupply is about to get slapped by reality'
items.idea: HFIR closed ARKK puts at $1.50 and $2.50 (two tranches) and recycled proceeds into BNO Dec 18 $60 calls (avg $2.57), on top of Jan-2027 BNO $60 calls bought at $5.70 that are now underwater. Thesis: the consensus Q4 oversupply narrative is wrong and physical tightness will force a re-rate. Author admits 'it's been a tough journey' across nine prior game-plan notes.
items.angle: Funding a long-crude view with short-growth-tech profits is a clean expression of the 'AI capex unwind + energy shock' barbell. Same night: drones on Ras Tanura and a Hormuz-east incident (Dark Side).
items.tweetA: Short ARKK, long Brent calls. That pair is basically a bet that 2027's problem is barrels, not tokens. Drones on Ras Tanura tonight and the oversupply crowd still hasn't flinched. $BNO $USO
items.tweetB: Everyone's oil model says Q4 surplus. Inventories just printed a 1.1M bbl build, smaller than expected, while Saudi intercepts drones over its biggest export terminal. When the surplus never shows up in the tanks, what's it a forecast of?

items.title: Gochujang cranberry sauce: Thanksgiving's menu is globalizing as Friendsgiving hands hosting to younger cohorts
items.idea: Smith argues the turkey-stuffing-cranberry canon feels like '1990s polygon graphics — good for the time'. Food-trend data shows gochujang, chili crisp, miso and harissa entering glazes and dressings, driven by younger Friendsgiving hosts. Globalized ingredient supply chains made it cheap; he wants celebrity-chef 'Mexican/Korean/Indian Thanksgiving' variants.
items.angle: Consumer signal: pantry share shifting to Asian/Middle Eastern condiments — tailwind for specialty-food CPG and grocery mix, headwind for legacy holiday SKUs.
items.tweetA: The most American meal of the year is quietly getting a gochujang glaze. When Friendsgiving hosts in their 20s rewrite the menu, 'ethnic aisle' stops being an aisle. Watch condiment share at $MKC and $GIS vs upstarts.
items.tweetB: Holiday menus change slowly, which is exactly why they're a good read on taste. Chili crisp in green bean casserole is a better adoption-curve indicator than any consumer survey.

items.title: Make Thanksgiving the holiday for celebrating immigration — 77% of Republicans agree the US is a 'nation of immigrants'
items.idea: Smith frames the Plymouth story as an immigration tale and argues Thanksgiving should become America's 'people' holiday versus July 4th's 'institutions' holiday. Polling: 77% of Republicans call the US a 'nation of immigrants', and immigration ranked third among themes Americans want new monuments for. He also proposes borrowing Japan's omiyage/White Day micro-gift culture for coworkers and neighbors.
items.angle: Cultural counterweight to restrictive immigration politics; the omiyage idea is effectively a pitch for a new low-ticket gifting season between Halloween and Christmas.
items.tweetA: 77% of Republicans say the US is a nation of immigrants. Policy says something else. That gap between identity and law usually closes eventually, and it's rarely the identity that moves.
items.tweetB: Japan built two separate gifting holidays (Valentine's for coworkers, White Day) basically out of chocolate marketing. A Thanksgiving omiyage habit would be the cheapest new retail season America could invent.

items.title: Trump: Jensen pardon 'always an option', and a government stake in Nvidia is 'probably not too late'
items.idea: In an NY Post interview Trump left a pardon on the table, told Huang not to plead the Fifth, and floated a state stake in Nvidia like the 10% Intel stake. WIRED reports an official told Intel rejection 'will have consequences'. Huang faces closed-door House interviews Tuesday and a public Senate Banking hearing Thursday Dec 3. Republicans and Democrats are both criticizing the reinstatement, and a more Democratic Congress arrives in January.
items.angle: A US equity stake in NVDA would reprice it as a quasi-national champion, which is bullish for policy support and bearish for governance discount and China access. Dec 3 is the next catalyst.
items.tweetA: A pardon is on the table for a CEO who hasn't been charged with anything, and the guy offering it also wants an equity stake. Intel was the template. If $NVDA becomes a state asset, model it like one: lower political risk, higher governance discount.
items.tweetB: Mark Dec 3: Jensen testifies before Senate Banking. The board can forgive him and the President can forgive him. Congress is the first audience that hasn't, and both parties are on the same side for once.

items.title: Jensen to staff: sorry, 90 min of therapy daily, monthly HR feedback, and no succession plan needed
items.idea: At an all-hands Huang apologized repeatedly, called it the second-hardest meeting of his life, and said he's in therapy 90 minutes a day with HR collecting monthly feedback for the board. Then: no succession plan, because of his 60-direct-report flat structure run for 33 years. Parekh notes 'succession' appears nowhere in Nvidia's annual report, and the family roles (daughter Madison as de facto chief of staff, son, son-in-law) went unmentioned.
items.angle: Key-man risk is now explicitly priced in credit (S&P cites succession). 60 direct reports and no successor is the structure lenders are flagging.
items.tweetA: 60 direct reports, 33 years, no successor, and he says that's the 'pride and joy.' That's exactly the line S&P quoted back in its negative watch. Equity calls it culture, credit calls it key-man risk. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The most valuable chip company on earth now runs with monthly HR reviews of its CEO going to the board. Has any trillion-dollar company tried probation for its founder before?

items.title: Nvidia's board: 'no way' to 'every confidence' in 11 days, unanimous both times
items.idea: Six days before reinstating Huang, chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to. It then voted unanimously to do the opposite. The changes: a chief compliance officer reporting to governance, a national security committee, and the investigation continuing. Two directors have served since 1993. NYT frames it as the board bowing to Trump; the WSJ editorial calls it 'Nvidia and Trump's State Capitalism'. Parekh compares it to OpenAI's Altman blip, where that board was remade within months.
items.angle: Activist and institutional pressure for a reconstituted board is the next shoe. A board refresh could be the catalyst that closes the governance discount and stops the CDS widening.
items.tweetA: Two unanimous votes in 11 days, in opposite directions. Two directors have been there since 1993. OpenAI's board after the Altman blip lasted a few months. I'd bet this one doesn't make it through proxy season intact. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The OpenAI blip took 5 days and the board got replaced. The Nvidia blip took 11 days and the board stayed. Markets forgave Altman's board turnover. They may not forgive the absence of one.

items.title: Meta's Muse handled ~half of all AI-agent shopping orders; Amazon ($69B ads) negotiating an end to the blockade
items.idea: Muse has 10M+ US/Canada users. In the week to Nov 22 it handled roughly half of AI-agent shopping orders, ahead of Grok and ChatGPT, and a quarter of users shop through it at $200+ per purchase on average. Amazon blocked it because agents bypass its ~$69B ad business, and now the two are discussing search and ad terms. Any deal needs sign-off from both Jassy and Zuckerberg. Banks are also locking out agents.
items.angle: Agentic commerce is the first real threat to retail media margins. Whatever toll Amazon gets from Muse sets the template for every agent and retailer deal.
items.tweetA: Amazon's $69B ad business exists because humans scroll search results. An agent doesn't scroll. Whatever toll Amazon charges Muse is the price of retail media in the agent era. $AMZN $META
items.tweetB: 10M Muse users, a quarter of them shopping at $200+ a ticket, and Meta already has half of agent checkout volume. Meta just did to agent shopping what Instagram did to mobile ads, and Amazon is the one asking for a deal.

items.title: Anthropic is now 'the Coke' of AI, public and over $1T market cap, while OpenAI slid to Pepsi
items.idea: Parekh's overall take: the Nvidia 'Mega-Blip 4.0' differs from the 2023 Altman blip and may take much longer to forget. He notes Anthropic is public with a market cap over $1T despite extreme volatility around its $83 IPO price (Dark Side: it briefly traded below $83 and recovered above it Wednesday). FT reports the tech sell-off deepening as the AI trade cracks.
items.angle: If a $1T+ name is swinging around its IPO price, AI listings act as a volatility sink. Use the IPO-price line as a sentiment gauge.
items.tweetA: A $1T company trading back and forth through its IPO price in one week. That isn't price discovery, it's the market working out whether frontier labs are utilities or options. The $83 line is the AI sentiment indicator now.
items.tweetB: Three years ago OpenAI was the Coke of AI. Now it's Pepsi, and the Coke is a public stock that briefly dipped under its IPO price. Brand leadership in AI lasts about as long as one model generation.

items.title: NDX briefly hit -20% (bear market) and the Dow was down 1,000+ points, then the dollar cracked at 11:15 and everything reversed
items.idea: Wednesday: the Nasdaq 100 touched bear-market territory (-20% from the high), NVDA fell 9%+ intraday and the Dow was down more than 1,000 points. The dollar started selling at ~11:15 ET, equities bottomed ~30 min later, and gold and crypto joined with a volume spike at the lows. Close: S&P near flat, Dow and R2K green, Nasdaq lagging. Candidate catalysts: FCC approval of SpaceX's orbital data centers, Burry reportedly closing his remaining NDX puts, a yen-carry squeeze. The author's verdict: no liquidity plus a dislocated market.
items.angle: The dollar led the turn, which makes DXY the tell for exhaustion. Three sessions with three personalities (+7%, reversal, near-bear then rip) is classic late-liquidation behavior.
items.tweetA: The order of the reversal matters: dollar breaks at 11:15, stocks bottom at 11:45, then gold and BTC rip. When the dollar leads equities off the lows, it's a funding story, not a fundamentals story. Watch DXY, not NVDA. $QQQ
items.tweetB: Nasdaq tagged -20% intraday, and by the close the Dow and Russell were green. +7%, then a reversal, then a near-bear rip in three sessions. That isn't a market making up its mind, it's one forced to keep changing it.

items.title: Hedge-fund net AI exposure at its lowest since Sep 2025; long/short ratio weakest since Oct 2024; AI shorts at multi-year highs
items.idea: Aggregate HF net exposure to AI stocks is at its lowest since September 2025, the AI long-to-short ratio is the weakest since October 2024, and AI short exposure as a share of gross is at multi-year highs. AI has gone from the most crowded long to a battleground, so squeezes cut both ways. Breadth Wednesday: ~340 S&P advancers vs ~150 decliners, equal-weight beating cap-weight, staples/REITs/dividend payers bid.
items.angle: Crowded-short AI plus rising breadth is a setup for violent squeezes in mega-cap AI while the equal-weight rotation continues. Pair trade: long RSP vs short QQQ on rips.
items.tweetA: A year ago the AI trade was too crowded to short. Now AI shorts are a multi-year high share of hedge fund gross. The crowding didn't go away, it switched sides. The next squeeze will be in names nobody wants to own.
items.tweetB: 340 advancers, 150 decliners, equal-weight beating cap-weight, staples bid. On a day the Nasdaq touched bear territory. Breadth says the rest of the market is fine. It's the index that's sick. $RSP $QQQ

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Total Pandemonium
items.title: Data-center credit spreads hit new records and stayed there, even as hyperscaler CDS eased
items.idea: Credit spreads widened sharply in the morning liquidation and then recovered with equities. Hyperscaler CDS came off fresh highs, but data-center credit spreads pushed to new records and didn't retrace. That's a split between cash-rich hyperscalers and the leveraged builders financing AI infrastructure. Equity can buy the dip on NVDA; a DC lender is underwriting construction cost, utilization and offtake.
items.angle: The divergence matters more than the index bounce. Leveraged DC operators and neoclouds are where refinancing stress shows first; watch $CRWV-type and DC ABS spreads.
items.tweetA: Hyperscaler CDS: off the highs. Data-center spreads: new record, no bounce. The stock market saw a rally Wednesday. The credit market saw a gap opening between who owns the cash and who owns the concrete.
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating whether $NVDA is cheap. The question that matters is whether the guy who borrowed against 50,000 GPUs and a 10-year lease can refinance in 2027. Data-center spreads at records say lenders have doubts.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Total Pandemonium
items.title: Treasuries rallied while crude rallied: the bond market is pivoting from inflation fear to growth fear (Dec 2018 parallel)
items.idea: Revised Q3 GDP, income, claims and new-home sales beat, durables and spending missed, and core PCE stayed hot. December still looks like a Fed hike. Yet yields fell across the curve and ignored the oil rally, with the front end pricing how much more tightening the economy can take. March hike expectations look vulnerable. Parallel: Powell's December 2018 hike into weak markets, followed by a pivot two weeks later. The IMF estimates a sharp AI-capex retrenchment cuts global GDP ~1.1% by 2028.
items.angle: Bonds rallying through an oil spike shows the regime has flipped to growth fear. A hike then pause is the setup that historically marks the end of a tightening cycle: long duration, long gold on the pivot.
items.tweetA: Oil up, core PCE hot, GDP beat, and Treasuries still rallied. When bonds ignore an energy shock, they're telling you which problem they think is bigger. December hike, March pause is the 2018 playbook.
items.tweetB: IMF: an AI capex retrenchment cuts global GDP by about 1.1% by 2028. For scale, the 2018 trade war was estimated at roughly 0.8%. The Fed is hiking into the one sector carrying US capex growth.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Total Pandemonium
items.title: Drones intercepted over Ras Tanura, tanker restrictions near UAE terminals, a maritime incident east of Hormuz, and Ukraine hitting Russian refineries
items.idea: Crude rallied despite growth fears. Saudi forces intercepted drones targeting Ras Tanura (critical refining and export hub), there were restrictions on tanker movements near UAE terminals and another maritime incident east of the Strait of Hormuz, and Ukrainian strikes hit Russian refineries again. US crude build was ~1.1M bbl, smaller than expected. The OPEC+ meeting is upcoming.
items.angle: Three separate Gulf-chokepoint signals in one session while equities obsess over Jensen. Refined product cracks are the cleanest exposure.
items.tweetA: Drones over Ras Tanura. Tankers restricted near UAE terminals. An incident east of Hormuz. Russian refineries on fire. All in one session, and the headline was a CEO's therapy schedule. Product cracks are where this shows up first. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: The market spent Wednesday on a $1T Nasdaq swing and barely noticed someone tried to hit the most important oil terminal on earth. That's a mispricing of attention, and attention usually catches up with the tape.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Total Pandemonium
items.title: Gold sold to $3,400 for liquidity, rebounded above $3,550; BTC surged toward $60K, but both still fragile until a Fed pivot
items.idea: In the panic, bullion was sold to raise cash and its usual links to yields and the dollar broke down. When the dollar weakened it bounced from ~$3,400 to above $3,550 but still finished lower. Bitcoin surged toward $60K as speculative appetite returned. Copper is weak on worries about the AI-driven industrial cycle. The author's view: a 'Trump put' can pause liquidation but doesn't ease dollar funding; only a Fed pivot that reaches credit changes the regime.
items.angle: Gold acting as the ATM in a margin call is typical of late-cycle deleveraging (2008, March 2020). It usually comes before gold's best leg once the CB pivots.
items.tweetA: Gold got sold to meet margin calls, as in Oct 2008 and March 2020. Both times it was materially higher 12 months later. Being an ATM in a panic is a setup, not the thesis breaking.
items.tweetB: A Trump put can stop a stock liquidation. It can't make dollar funding cheaper. That's why gold bounced $150 and still closed red. The metal is waiting for the Fed, not the White House.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AA, For Now
items.title: S&P puts Nvidia's AA on negative watch; 5Y CDS touched 147bp vs ~40bp in June
items.idea: S&P placed Nvidia's AA on CreditWatch negative, citing governance, board independence, executive oversight and founder dependence, and had already cut its management and governance assessment from positive to neutral. 5Y CDS briefly hit 147.27bp (from ~40bp in June and ~82bp by late July), so protection on $10M rose from ~$40K to ~$147K a year. Moody's had already moved its outlook from positive to stable at Aa1. A one-notch cut is possible within 90 days unless the investigations show material damage.
items.angle: An AA name at 147bp trades like a BBB. The CDS-vs-rating gap is the trade, with the real transmission running through NVDA's guarantees.
items.tweetA: Nvidia is rated AA. Its 5Y CDS is at 147bp. Plenty of BBB companies trade tighter than that. The agencies are just now catching up to what the swaps were pricing in July. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Insuring $10M of Nvidia debt cost $40K a year in June. Now it's $147K. The balance sheet didn't change. What changed is the market realizing Nvidia's credit is being lent out to the rest of the AI economy.

charts.desc: 🔥 Nvidia 5-year CDS spread (ICE Data Services): ~40bp in June to 147bp, with steady widening since summer, well before the governance scandal

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AA, For Now
items.title: The 'Bank of Nvidia': $118B in guarantees, including $105B of credit support for land, power and shell at the Portspike campus
items.idea: Q3 disclosures show Nvidia guarantees of about $118B, including ~$105B of credit support tied to land, power and shell capacity at the Portspike campus, on top of supply, cloud and equity commitments. A one-notch downgrade is a nuisance for NVDA itself (Moody's sees $240B+ cash by FY2028), but lenders to guaranteed borrowers may demand more spread or collateral. Question: who guarantees the guarantor?
items.angle: Contingent liabilities are the real exposure. Anyone holding DC project debt wrapped by NVDA guarantees is short NVDA's rating.
items.tweetA: $118B of guarantees, $105B of it backing land, power and shells at one campus. Nvidia isn't only selling GPUs, it's lending its AA to the companies that buy them. A downgrade doesn't hurt Nvidia. It hurts everyone borrowing against its name.
items.tweetB: Vendor financing has a history. Lucent and Nortel guaranteed customer debt in 1999–2000 to keep orders flowing. The numbers are bigger now and the balance sheet is far stronger, but the reflexivity works the same way.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — AA, For Now
items.title: Goldman: $320B of chip and compute financing in 2027, ~7x this year, mostly via chipmaker-guaranteed structures
items.idea: Goldman credit strategists expect ~$320B in chip and compute financing in 2027, nearly 7x the 2026 pace, much of it through structures backed by chipmaker guarantees rather than direct bonds. Chipmakers have issued under $35B of bonds, with ~$94B index-eligible outstanding, so hedgers use CDS. The chipmaker CDS-bond basis went from below zero a year ago to ~75bp, vs ~45bp for hyperscalers. AI IG spreads are ~40bp wider than comparable non-AI paper.
items.angle: With a 7x jump in off-balance-sheet AI financing and too few bonds to hedge with, the CDS basis is the stress gauge to track. Relative value: short chipmaker CDS basis vs hyperscalers.
items.tweetA: $320B of AI chip financing next year, 7x this year, and the guarantors have under $35B of their own bonds outstanding. When the hedge market is that much smaller than the exposure, CDS stops being insurance and becomes the price signal.
items.tweetB: AI IG paper trades ~40bp wide of non-AI IG at the same rating. The market has created a new credit category: 'AA, but AI.' That premium is the market's estimate of how much of this capex never earns its cost of capital.

items.title: 'AI' mentions on mega-cap calls fell 27% to 265, the lowest since ChatGPT's launch quarter
items.idea: Bespoke counts 'AI' on AAPL, AMZN, META, MSFT, GOOGL and NVDA calls. The total fell from 364 to 265 (-27%), the lowest since Q4 2022. GOOGL led with 73, then AMZN 47, AAPL 44, MSFT 38, META 35, NVDA 28. Apple was the only increase (43 to 44, its own high).
items.angle: Falling hype-word frequency during a capex boom suggests the narrative is moving from vision to ROI defense. It's a soft signal that the 'AI story premium' is being priced out.
items.tweetA: AI mentions on mega-cap calls are down 27% to the lowest since ChatGPT launched, while capex guides keep rising. Talking about it less while spending more on it is what an industry does when the questions shift from 'how big' to 'how much does it earn'.
items.tweetB: Google said 'AI' 73 times. Apple said it 44 times, a record. Nvidia said it 28. If you'd been told in 2023 which of these would be the lowest in 2026, you'd have bet on Apple.

items.title: NVDA's AI mentions fell 80% from 154 to 28; Apple out-mentioned Nvidia for the first time since 2021
items.idea: NVDA peaked at 154 mentions in Q3 2023, still the high for any of the six. This quarter it dropped 57 to 28, the lowest since Q2 2022. Analysts pressed interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress on pricing power, how far NVDA would go financing customers' data centers, talent retention through the leadership change, and policy risk to 2028 growth.
items.angle: The analyst questions changed from demand to margins, customer financing and governance. That lines up with S&P's watch and the $118B guarantees.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's earnings call: 154 AI mentions in 2023, 28 now. The analysts stopped asking where demand comes from and started asking how much Nvidia will finance its customers. That change in questions says more than the count.
items.tweetB: When a company's Q&A moves from 'how big is the TAM' to 'will you keep financing the customers,' the TAM is no longer the problem. The balance sheet is.

items.title: FCC clears SpaceX for up to 1M data-processing satellites (Starmind); 100K must be deployed by Nov 2035
items.idea: The FCC approval allows up to 1M orbital data-processing satellites, a cap rather than a count, with a 100,000-satellite deployment deadline of November 2035. SpaceX has leased ground compute to Anthropic since May. No launches, operating capacity or funding for Starmind have been disclosed. Fulcrum: value Starmind as a separate line from the ground DCs. The approval was also one of the candidate catalysts for Wednesday's intraday reversal.
items.angle: Orbital compute is now a regulated, licensable asset class. The financing structure, not launch cost, decides whether it's a business.
items.tweetA: The FCC just licensed a million orbiting data centers. The binding constraint isn't launch cost anymore, Starship is fixing that. It's whether a bank will lend against a GPU it can never repossess.
items.tweetB: 1M satellites approved, 100K due by Nov 2035. That's ~10K a year, every year, roughly the size of today's entire Starlink fleet annually. The license reads less like a permit and more like a production target.

items.title: Lenders tried to bar SpaceX from launching $40B of pledged chips into orbit, because collateral in space has no recovery value
items.idea: FT (Nov 20): lenders sought to stop SpaceX launching $40B of pledged chips into orbit to protect collateral. On Earth, a defaulted GPU can be seized and resold. In orbit, recovery depends on a buyer taking over and operating the satellite in place. Apollo/Goldman priced a separate $44B SpaceX GPU financing. The counter-case: long-dated, enforceable take-or-pay contracts from a creditworthy customer could make hardware resale value irrelevant.
items.angle: This sets the template for space-infrastructure finance: contract-backed, not asset-backed. Equity will have to fund more of Starmind than the ground business.
items.tweetA: Collateral has an escape velocity. The same $40B of GPUs is bankable on Earth and nearly unsecured in orbit. Space compute will be financed like a satellite operator, on contracts, not like a data center on hardware.
items.tweetB: $44B of SpaceX GPU debt priced by Apollo and Goldman, and the lenders' main condition is 'keep it on the ground.' The market for orbital compute is now limited less by physics than by the repo man.

items.title: Q3 GDP 4.3% strengthens the hike case; Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 partners incl. China and EU
items.idea: Roundup: the US economy grew 4.3% in Q3, and elevated inflation strengthens the case for another Fed increase (Semafor). Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU (Guardian). VP Vance says he was assured Huang is not under federal investigation (CBS).
items.angle: 4.3% growth plus new tariffs plus a hike while equities sit near bear territory is a stagflation-lite mix. Tariffs are a new shock for the EU and China.
items.tweetA: 4.3% GDP, a Fed preparing to hike, and a new round of tariffs on 14 countries, while the Nasdaq flirts with a bear market. The economy has never looked stronger in the data, and the market is pricing the next 12 months instead.
items.tweetB: New tariffs on China and the EU the same week the Fed signals a hike. Tariffs are a supply shock, and a hike is a demand cure for it. That's the wrong medicine for the problem, delivered on a schedule.

items.title: Leaked Russian government data (BBC): 490,000+ Russian soldiers dead since Feb 2022
items.idea: BBC analysis of leaked Russian government data suggests more than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Also: judges in Netanyahu's six-year corruption trial recommended prosecutors drop the most serious charge, and Kilmar Ábrego García arrived in Madrid after choosing to leave the US.
items.angle: A death toll that high strains Russian labor markets and the demographic base. It's a wage-inflation and recruitment-bonus story inside Russia, and a factor in any ceasefire talk.
items.tweetA: 490,000 Russian soldiers dead, mostly working-age men, in a country already shrinking. Russia's labor shortage and wage inflation make more sense once you see that number.
items.tweetB: 490K dead per Russia's own leaked data. Compare the ~15K Soviet deaths in 10 years of Afghanistan. The Kremlin's political tolerance for losses is the variable most ceasefire models underrate.

items.title: GDPx leaderboard: GPT-6.2 Astra 19.3%, Fable 5.2 16.4%, Gemini 4 Carbon 10.9%; 'Twitter vibes measure pleasantness, not IQ'
items.idea: SemiAnalysis's GDPx has 206 tasks across 11 frontier domains (chip design, cyber, bio, finance, legal, quant, RSI, hardware, materials, alignment, SWE), built with 14 data partners. Opus 5.5 led at launch with just 12%. Now OpenAI's 6.2 Astra is #1 (19.3%), Fable 5.2 #2 (16.4%), Gemini 4 Carbon #5 (10.9%) and Neon #6 (10.1%). Without the safety-classifier domains and with partial grading, it's 32.2% vs 29.9%. OpenAI dominates the cost-performance Pareto frontier. SemiAnalysis says it was wrong to predict DeepMind's demise, but Google is still a 'distant third' tier.
items.angle: The labs are separating by spiky capability, not overall quality. Enterprise model routing by domain is the coming default, which favors multi-model orchestration layers.
items.tweetA: The model X calls 'the worst OpenAI ever released' tops the hardest frontier benchmark at 19.3%. The influencer test is 'is it nice to code with.' The money test is 'can it do chip design and M&A.' Those are now different models.
items.tweetB: Best model on GDPx scores 19%. Six weeks ago the best was 12%. That's +60% in a month and a half on a benchmark built to be unsaturated. Plot that line before you decide AI progress is stalling.

charts.desc: 🔥 GDPx leaderboard (all domains), leaderboard excluding safety-classifier domains with partial grading, and cost-performance Pareto frontier (OpenAI dominates, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at the low end)

items.title: Fable 5.2 costs $88 and 1.23M output tokens per task, 1.9x GPT-6.2 Astra, but triples Opus 5.5 at SWE (24.4% vs 8.9%)
items.idea: Fable 5.2 is by far the most expensive to run: $88 and 1.23M output tokens per task, 1.9x the cost of 6.2 Astra with 3.9x the tokens, driven by persistence and subagent spawning. Materials: $79 for 21.8% vs Astra 41.3%, and Sol 25.8% at $8. Finance (partial grading): Fable 53.6%, Opus 5.5 54.6%, Astra 53.5%, but Fable is 6.6x Astra's cost. SWE: Fable 24.4% vs Opus 8.9% vs Sol 15.6%, at 17x Sol's cost. RSI: Astra 33.2% vs Fable 24.1%, which SemiAnalysis attributes to Anthropic deliberately nerfing research ability.
items.angle: Agentic persistence is driving token demand per task up. Bullish for inference compute volume even when per-token prices fall. Output tokens per task is the inference capex metric.
items.tweetA: One coding task: 1.23M output tokens, $88. The frontier is getting smarter by thinking longer and spawning subagents, not by getting cheaper. Anyone modeling inference demand off falling per-token prices is missing the 4x token multiplier. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: On materials science, a $8 model beats an $79 model, 25.8% to 21.8%. 'Best model' is now a per-domain routing problem, and whoever owns the router captures the margin.

items.title: Google's weak prompt caching made Gemini 4 Neon 18–32% more expensive to run than it needed to be
items.idea: Running Neon on GDPx cost $15,286. At Opus 5.5's cache-hit rate it would have been $12,536 (-18%), at 6.2 Astra's $10,403 (-32%). Google shipped a caching update the same day (+4.5% hit rate, ~17-18% cheaper). SemiAnalysis says Neon's popularity comes from behavior, not intelligence ('reminds us of GPT-4o'), and that models are rapidly becoming superhuman at optimizing inference stacks, so the gap should close.
items.angle: Serving-stack quality, not just chip cost, is now a 20–30% unit-cost lever. Look for inference-software moats, and expect TPU economics to improve as Google catches up.
items.tweetA: Same model, same tasks, 32% cheaper with better prompt caching. In inference, the serving software is now worth as much as a chip generation. Google shipped a fix the same day that cuts Neon's bill another ~17%. $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Gemini 4 Neon is the most-loved model and a distant third on hard tasks. It's GPT-4o again: users reward cheerfulness, and benchmarks reward capability. The revenue goes to whichever one enterprises end up paying for.

items.title: Qwen4-Max best Chinese model at 7.44%; Kimi K3.1 'benchmaxxed' on Terminal Bench; custom cyber post-trains rising as labs tighten classifiers
items.idea: Qwen4-Max scores 7.44% on GDPx, a bit below Claude Sonnet 5.5 but much cheaper, with its biggest gains in SWE, RSI, cyber and bio. Kimi K3.1 Pro is #1 on Terminal Bench but underperforms on GDPx, which SemiAnalysis calls benchmaxxing (TB is 10% of the AA index). As Anthropic, OpenAI and Google restrict cyber and bio, domain-specific post-trains are gaining. Hinoki's HO1 (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash cyber tune) did marginally better, while 'abliterated' Kimi and DeepSeek did slightly worse, because vanilla OSS models never refused to begin with.
items.angle: Safety classifiers at frontier labs are creating a legitimate market for specialized and open models in cyber and bio, which is a regulatory flashpoint. Chinese models remain a cost-tier, not a frontier-tier, competitor.
items.tweetA: Frontier labs keep tightening cyber classifiers. Result: the best way to get a cyber task done is an open-weight Chinese base model with a custom post-train. Safety at the frontier is pushing capability to the edge of the ecosystem.
items.tweetB: Kimi K3.1 is #1 on Terminal Bench and well behind on a benchmark it didn't optimize for. Every public leaderboard turns into a target eventually. Private evals are where actual capability shows up.

items.title: Q3 GDP: real private demand +5.8%, best in five years
items.idea: Ryan Detrick: 'best GDP print in years. Real private demand soared 5.8%, best in five years.' Backward-looking, but it comes as the Nasdaq trades near bear-market levels.
items.angle: Strong final private demand into a tech bear is the 2018 setup: economy fine, financial conditions doing the tightening. It makes the Fed hike more likely, which is the risk.
items.tweetA: Real private demand +5.8%, a five-year high, in the same week the Nasdaq touched -20%. The last time the economy and tech diverged this much, the Fed hiked into it (Dec 2018) and reversed within weeks.
items.tweetB: The economy just printed its best private demand in five years and nobody is celebrating. Markets don't price the quarter that's over. They price what the next Fed hike does to the quarter that's coming.

items.title: Goldman: hedge-fund AI short exposure as % of global gross at multi-year highs
items.idea: Goldman Prime data (via @blakemillardcfa): aggregate short exposure to AI stocks as a percentage of total global gross exposure is at multi-year highs. It matches Dark Side's read on hedge-fund net AI exposure at its lowest since Sep 2025.
items.angle: Two independent sources confirm AI is now a crowded short. That raises squeeze risk around any positive catalyst (Jensen's Dec 3 testimony, the Fed).
items.tweetA: AI short exposure is at multi-year highs as a share of hedge fund gross. Squeezes need three things: crowded shorts, thin liquidity, a catalyst. Two are already here. The third is on the calendar for Dec 3 and Dec 10.
items.tweetB: Hedge funds were most long AI at the top and most short it now. Wednesday's intraday reversal was a preview of what a crowded short does in a thin tape.

items.title: NDX 6-month relative performance vs SPX at -8.7%, through the -8.5% threshold, a rare extreme since 1985
items.idea: The Nasdaq-100's 6-month relative performance vs the S&P 500 hit -8.7% and fell further Wednesday. Daily Chartbook studies every first cross below -8.5% in six months since 1985, with forward returns in the full study.
items.angle: Extreme relative underperformance by NDX has historically mean-reverted, or marked regime changes (2000, 2022). Which one depends on credit.
items.tweetA: NDX vs SPX over 6 months: -8.7%, one of the most extreme readings since 1985. Sometimes that kept going (2000), sometimes it snapped back. What separated them was credit, and data-center spreads are at records.
items.tweetB: Three years of 'just own the Nasdaq' and it's now trailing the S&P by nearly 9 points in six months. Mean reversion is the base rate, but base rates don't account for $118B of vendor guarantees.

items.title: Zweig Breadth Thrust clock: 10-day EMA at 49.25%, nearly halfway to the 61.5% trigger
items.idea: @hbresearchx: the ZBT setup is on track. The 10-day EMA of breadth has risen every day this week to 49.25%, almost halfway to the 61.5% trigger. The window is 10 sessions from a sub-40% reading.
items.angle: A ZBT trigger is one of the strongest bullish breadth signals historically. Combined with equal-weight outperformance, it's the bull case for broadening, not mega-cap AI.
items.tweetA: Zweig Breadth Thrust EMA at 49.25%, needs 61.5%. It's one of the rarest and most reliable buy signals there is, and it would fire while the Nasdaq sits near a bear market. That's the market telling you leadership is changing, not that the bull is over. $RSP
items.tweetB: Breadth improving every day this week while AI megacaps bleed. If the ZBT triggers, it'll be the first one in memory led by staples and REITs instead of tech.

items.title: Timmer: 5-year earnings CAGR peaking at 15%; history says it reverts toward ~7%
items.idea: Jurrien Timmer (Fidelity): the 5-year EPS CAGR is peaking at ~15%, in line with most earnings cycles since the 1930s. Bloomberg consensus for the next 5 quarters keeps it in the low double digits. If that holds, current multiples are 'a deal', but historically, once the peak is in, growth returns to ~7%.
items.angle: Multiples rest on growth persistence. If CAGR halves to 7%, fair multiples compress, especially for AI names whose growth is most capex-dependent.
items.tweetA: 5-year EPS CAGR at 15%, a peak seen roughly once a cycle since the 1930s. Consensus assumes it stays double-digit. History says ~7%. The difference between those two is about 5 turns of P/E.
items.tweetB: Every earnings cycle since the 1930s peaks around 15% 5-year CAGR, then halves. This one comes with $320B of debt-financed chip capex attached. If growth normalizes, the debt doesn't.
